name: Sin, evil, and universal salvation
plain_explanation: John the Scot holds that sin arises from human freedom -- man turning toward himself instead of toward God -- and that evil is not a positive thing with its own ground, but a privation of good, and therefore, strictly, a form of not-being. Following Origen, he holds that even the devils will eventually be saved, though later than other beings, and that eternal punishment is not truly eternal.
precise_definition: Evil as privatio boni (privation of good) rather than a substantial or created reality; combined with the doctrine of eventual universal salvation (apocatastasis), including of fallen angels.
why_it_mattered: This combination -- evil as mere absence, and salvation as ultimately universal -- was doctrinally suspect, since it seemed to undercut the orthodox doctrine of eternal damnation.
historical_origin: The salvation-of-devils doctrine is explicitly traced by Russell to Origen; the privation account of evil has roots in Neoplatonism (evil as absence of the Good) as mediated through Augustine and the pseudo-Dionysius.
examples: "Like Origen, John holds that even the devils will be saved at last, though later than other people."
competing_positions: Saint Augustine's view of eternal damnation without hope of relief, which Russell notes John the Scot's account of the sexless, purely spiritual resurrected body directly contrasts with
connection_to_politics_or_religion: Directly heretical relative to orthodox eschatology.
